1:
Where the chapter begins is disputed. Gill reports that some join these verses to the close of the preceding chapter and thinks they rather begin a new section; Henry notes the same opinion; Clarke says the first five allude to the last and puts the new section at the sixth verse. Calvin rejects the join: a new subject is before us, God seeking reconciliation as a husband would with an unchaste wife. Keil and Delitzsch alone follow it through, on a grammatical ground: the opening infinitive cannot begin a new train of thought, so it must hang on the verb of rejection before it.

That opening word has puzzled everyone. Keil and Delitzsch record that the Greek and Syriac leave it untranslated, that Jerome renders it as a thing commonly said, and that the reading making it I might say is hardly justifiable. Calvin notes the same omission and settles on the sense of supposing a case: the divorce law is stated as men state it, then overtopped — I will surpass whatever kindness there is among men, and receive thee back.

Wesley states the law flatly: he cannot take her again by statute, yet I am ready to be reconciled. Ellicott adds that the recent finding of the book of the law had probably given the prohibition fresh prominence, and that the earlier prophet of this figure had done what the law forbade and held out hope of return, while Jeremiah must play a sterner part. He records, and refuses, the reading of many who take the closing invitation as an indignant exclamation and so as rejection.

The Arabian at the wayside divides them. Clarke and Ellicott make him a robber, the lawless desert tribes lying in ambush, Clarke having him rise in the saddle where there is no cover, watching for the smoke or dust that betrays a caravan. Wesley makes him a trader, pitching his tent by the roadside to meet passing customers. Calvin turns the image on the hearers as their own judges — name a hill where thou hast not been — noting that strumpets seek hiding places while these sought hilltops. Henry draws the pastoral use: in repentance it is good to reflect on the places and companies where the sin was committed.

The withheld rain is chastisement, though the calendar wobbles. Gill sets the former rain in the month answering to October and the latter in that answering to March; Clarke dates them to early November and mid-April. Ellicott reverses the seasons, putting the showers in spring and the latter rain in autumn, and supplies a drought in Josiah's reign. Calvin's interest is the hardness, not the dates: the drought was so uncommon that a particle of sound mind would have seen God was at war with them, and they were not subdued at all.

Whether the cry My father is welcomed or exposed is the sharpest split. Keil and Delitzsch date the from this time to Josiah's reformation and call the appeal lip-service, the life being unamended. Ellicott corrects the tense to hast thou not cried, and hears a stern irony painting a surface repentance. Gill sets out the hypocrisy reading — calling God Father while worshipping idols — but prefers to hear grace, God putting the words of return into their mouths. Calvin calls that reading incorrect: God does not wait for repentance but of his own accord meets and allures the apostates; Clarke and Wesley take it as invitation too. The questions about anger are given by Gill and Ellicott as part of that put speech, by Calvin as God arguing from his own nature in the third person, and by Clarke as a retort — why should wrath not continue while transgression does? Ellicott notes that the word anger is not in the Hebrew, and suspects both verses are quoted from penitential litanies the people had used.
6:
A second discourse begins, and every voice dates it. Gill notes that Jeremiah began prophesying in Josiah's thirteenth year; Clarke places this after the eighteenth; Ellicott calls it a second sermon under the same king, comparing the two kingdoms' guilt. Henry insists the date makes it intelligible: Josiah was hearty in his reformation and the people were not sincere, and the address is aimed at that hypocrisy. Calvin generalises — when rulers labour to purge worship there are always many who dissemble while the old antipathy remains. Ellicott adds that backsliding is stronger in Hebrew, a noun rather than an adjective: apostasy is personified, and she does not merely go up to the hills but keeps going.

What God said next divides them. Gill has him sending to Israel by the earlier prophets, and Clarke lists them by name. Calvin reports both readings and inclines the same way, that God recalled the ten tribes by his servants and spent his labour in vain. Keil and Delitzsch refuse it: the words are not a summons but a thought God had to himself; he did call Israel by prophets, but that is not in view. Ellicott reaches the same result by the verb, which may be second or third person — thou shalt return, or she will return — and prefers the latter as a hope rather than a demand.

The next clause is a textual crux, and the two grammarians take opposite sides. Ellicott follows a conjectural emendation and reads and she saw, which he thinks gives a better sense. Keil and Delitzsch report that proposal, from Graf with Ewald and the Syriac, and Jerome's outright omission, and reject both: either change buries what Judah saw in a subordinate clause and halves the preceding verse. Gill and Calvin keep the received reading — not Judah only saw, but God, who sees all things, saw the idolatry and its causes, so Judah surpassed her sister not through ignorance but deliberate wickedness.

How the divorce was executed they agree on. Clarke and Wesley make it the giving up into Assyrian hands, Wesley adding that God there took from her the title of his church. Ellicott hears in the wording's technical fulness the opening formula of a real writing of divorcement, reciting the husband's alleged causes. Calvin raises the difficulty nobody else does: how can a bill of divorce be said to have been given when God denies through another prophet that he ever gave one?

The lightness of her whoredom is disputed as a word. Gill offers swiftness, the thing running through the land as one took it from another, or else a trivial offence. Calvin reads levity; Clarke passes the word over for the grossness of the idolatry. Keil and Delitzsch work the spelling — the defective form is a Masoretic pointer to lightness, but the word for voice is also written defectively at times, and lightness makes a poor predicate for a whoredom that pollutes a land. Ellicott begins with levity and ends preferring the same alternative, a cry, as the cry of the cities of the plain was said to be great.

Why Judah was worse is the sermon's point. Keil and Delitzsch give the mechanism: the reformation restored the temple worship outwardly while the heart clave to the idols, so the returning was not from the whole heart. Ellicott says Judah had looked on her sister with contemptuous scorn and is taught otherwise, her repentance simulated, made with a lie. Calvin anticipates the objection — is the land not cleansed, is God not worshipped by the law? — and answers that they should have grown wise by their brethren's fall. On the verdict Clarke and Ellicott reach independently for one comparison: as the humbled publican went home justified rather than the boasting Pharisee, so the renegade put in the better plea, open rebellion standing higher than hypocrisy.
12:
The message is aimed north, and the aiming is discussed. Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott name the ground: Assyria and the cities of the Medes, whither the ten tribes had been carried. Gill and Calvin both notice the geographical difficulty and answer it alike: the exiles lay scattered eastward, but the capital of the empire that took them lay north. Gill denies any journey — against the Targum, go expresses a command and the prophet's readiness rather than local motion, and he read the words in Jerusalem before the elders of Judah as if Israel stood there. Henry makes the facing a rebuke: the prophet looks that way to show God had not forgotten them, and to upbraid the men of Judah, who would hear a call no better than men hundreds of miles off.

Ellicott catches what the English cannot: the summons is an assonance, turn back thou that hast turned away, and the threat withheld is literally the face, so awful in its wrath.

The one condition is confession, and the particle carrying it is disputed. Gill takes only at face value and presses its smallness: it is all that is insisted on, the least that can be done. Ellicott calls it the one sufficient condition, the confession that keeps nothing back and makes no excuses. Calvin prefers to render the word yet rather than only: hypocrites reason that God is so ready to recall sinners that matters are easily settled, so with every promise of favour an exhortation to repentance must be joined. Keil and Delitzsch give the next phrase its force — scattered thy ways is hither and thither, on many a track, after strange gods — Ellicott having it as leaving traces everywhere, Wesley as running here and there to idols.

The marriage is reasserted rather than dissolved. Wesley reads it as covenant, ready to be renewed notwithstanding the unfaithfulness; Ellicott as pity offering pardon to the adulterous wife, noting that the prophet has dropped the parable, or rather fused sign with thing signified. Gill dwells on the paradox — backsliders and yet children, the relation continuing through monstrous ingratitude — and turns it into an inventory of how God's own people backslide: love waxing cold, private prayer restrained and public worship neglected, bad company and gross sin. Calvin's wonder is at the repetition: God, finding his kindness neglected, does not reject the slothful but adds new stimulants and invites again.

How many will come divides the two Methodists. Clarke reads the one of a city and two of a family as a floor: if one only is left, or willing, and two of a whole tribe, yet these will be received and brought home. Wesley reads the words the opposite way, as a promise that none is missed: being married to them, God will find them out though there be but one in a city. Ellicott sizes the terms instead, family being the wider word, a clan taking in many cities, and sets the limitation beside the older prophet's remnant. Clarke turns aside to protest that he has heard the words most sinfully applied to prove an eternal decree electing one out of a city and two out of a family and leaving the rest to perish — by men professing to believe in one who tasted death for every man.

Where Zion is divides them too. Clarke keeps it literal, a bringing back from captivity into their land. Wesley argues from history: the ten tribes never did return, so the going up must be spiritual, when all Israel shall be saved. Henry reads the passage as gospel — the church founded by gathering the scattered children of God, the ceremonial law superseded, Jews and Gentiles united as Israel and Judah are here. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the increase of a saved remnant is a constant feature of the Messianic picture.
15:
Who the promised pastors are is the sharpest disagreement here, and it runs across the schools. Gill excludes political rulers by name: these are ministers of the word, chiefly the apostles, with a lesser fulfilment in those who rebuilt after the return. Ellicott excludes the other side, taking the word as before of kings and rulers and not of priests, hearing David behind the phrase according to mine heart, and reading the promise as a return to the pattern of the ideal ruler. Clarke will not choose — the pastor means king or prophet, and the promise may cover either or both, men of God's own choosing. Calvin allows faithful magistrates in but refers it chiefly to prophets and priests, grounding it in a diagnosis: the people were ruined because instruction had ceased and their pastors had become mute dogs.

The abolition of the ark draws the boldest comment in the chapter. Ellicott calls the verse noteworthy for its exceeding boldness and finds in it the germ of the new covenant: the centre of Israel's worship, the symbol and seemingly more than the symbol of the divine presence, is to pass away as the brazen serpent had, Jeremiah being foremost among the prophets in seeing that God fulfils himself in many ways. Clarke says the same practically — the pledge is no longer necessary, worship confined to no one place or people, and if the ark is lost it is never rebuilt. Wesley extends it to the whole ceremonial system, of which the ark was shadow and Christ substance.

Calvin thinks nobody has understood the verse: interpreters have perverted it and none have seen the design. He dismisses as frigid and wholly foreign the old gloss that the ark would no more be carried out to battle because no enemy would invade; the passage is about the kingdom of Christ. Ellicott records a legend that Jeremiah hid the tabernacle and ark in a cave to be restored in the latter days, a story sitting oddly against the verse it attaches to.

Jerusalem as the throne divides the readers from the historian. Gill takes it for the Gospel church; Clarke for the universal church, God enthroned wherever the Lamb is acknowledged; Wesley for the church typified by the city, in place of the ark. Ellicott alone keeps the prophet inside his own horizon: the title had belonged in popular speech to the ark where God dwelt between the cherubim, the prophet extends it to the whole city, and it was not given him to see what even the apostles were slow to learn, that there is no holy city on earth. He adds that imagination is better rendered stubbornness.

The reunion is read alike as to substance and disputed as to a preposition. Gill has the two houses joined in one Gospel church state; Wesley says the kingdoms become one; Clarke gives the prophecy two aspects, the return from Babylon and the days of Christianity, the Jews gathered at last not from Chaldea only but from the whole earth. Calvin makes it historical: the seed of Abraham had been torn asunder and the hatred was inveterate; the fruit of exile would be a return not to the old emulation but to calling on God together. On the preposition Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch differ — Ellicott renders walk to rather than with, Judah seeking Israel's alliance, where Keil and Delitzsch keep the sense of walking upon.

Three of them notice the same startling assumption: Judah's own exile is taken as accomplished. Keil and Delitzsch mark it assumed though the fall of city and temple was only implied a verse before; Ellicott says the words foresee a like exile in the north for Judah; Calvin presses hardest, that the Jews had not yet gone anywhere but sat quiet in their own nest, unconvinced of what they afterwards found true to their loss.
19:
The verse opening the last movement is read two ways. Ellicott insists the How shall I put thee is an exclamation, not a question — a promise uttered with intensity of affirmation — and denies what follows is an answer, calling it the same thought continued; Keil and Delitzsch agree. Clarke builds the verse on the opposite structure, a question with its reply: how can ye be accounted a holy seed, being polluted? — to which Thou shalt call me My father answers. Wesley agrees a condition is laid down: esteem thee as my child till thou show some proof of repentance. Calvin hears a different question — how could the race of Abraham be propagated when nearly dead — asked so the Jews should feel their case past remedy. Even the heritage is disputed: Ellicott renders it a heritage of the beauty of beauties of the nations and says the English confuses that word with the similar one for hosts — just where Wesley builds, taking the hosts for Gentiles.

Then the charge returns. Gill and Henry both press the figure of a wife leaving the friend who provided for her, and Henry sharpens it: to deal treacherously with men is bad enough, but so to deal with God is treason. Calvin makes the severity toward Israel a device aimed at Judah, too hardened to think the example meant them, and reads the weeping on the heights the same way: the Israelites had not yet wept so, and the prophet sets before the Jews the tears prepared for them. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott hear the sound as present, the prophet already overhearing on those heights the weeping of suppliant prayers.

Clarke sets the confession out as a five-part argument; Ellicott hears a dramatic form, almost a litany, and notes the repetition the English loses — turn, ye children that have turned, I will heal your turnings.

The hills and the multitude of mountains defeat everyone differently. Gill offers a fortification of encompassing hills, or the idols worshipped on them; Wesley takes the idols and their sacrifices. Calvin makes the confession psychological: we thought there was more defence in many gods than in one, and the deception ruined us. Ellicott says the italics betray the difficulty and, from revelry, wealth and multitude, prefers revelry: the wild ritual on the high places brought loss, not gain. Keil and Delitzsch report the older construction making it the tumult of the mountains, taken for the many gods.

Whether the shame is Baal or sin at large divides them. Clarke says the word signifies Baal, the thing that brought them into contempt and ruin; Ellicott presses further, noting the article and the name-pairs in which the word substitutes for Baal, and reading the verse as a prodigal waste of victims. Keil and Delitzsch agree, then correct the inference: the idols devoured flocks and children not because these were sacrificed, since sheep and oxen were offered to the LORD too, but because idolatry drew down the invasions that ate them. Calvin and Wesley keep it general — wickedness, of which they ought to be ashamed; sin, which brought shame first into the world. Gill lists the Jewish reading of Baal and adds his own: the shame may be the rejecting and crucifying of the Messiah, repented of at the future conversion.

They end lying down, and even the posture has a tense. Keil and Delitzsch insist it is not we lie but we will lay ourselves down, as a man in grief throws himself on the ground, disgrace enwrapping him like mourning dress. Ellicott agrees, giving the sense of penitents accepting sentence: we chose the shameful thing, therefore let us bear our shame. Calvin surveys the versions, some past and some future, and settles on the present. Henry adds that true penitents learn to call sin shame, even the sin that pleased them most.
